title: Advancing regulatory variant effect prediction with AlphaGenome
generated_by: ChatGPT GPT-6; notes grounded in uploaded PDF
source_note: Sequential notes follow the article section order; info gives supporting detail and concl gives a takeaway when warranted. Methods notes follow main text.

items.q: What does AlphaGenome aim to solve?
items.a: Sequence-to-function models often trade long genomic context for nucleotide-level resolution and specialize in only a few assay modalities. AlphaGenome seeks to combine all three: long context, fine resolution, and diverse predictions.
items.concl: A unified model could help interpret non-coding variants through several regulatory mechanisms at once.

items.q: What are AlphaGenome’s inputs and outputs?
items.a: It takes 1 Mb of human or mouse DNA and predicts 5,930 human or 1,128 mouse tracks across 11 modalities, at resolutions up to 1 bp.
items.info: Outputs include RNA-seq, CAGE, PRO-cap, accessibility, histone marks, TF binding, splicing and contact maps.

items.q: What is the headline benchmark result?
items.a: AlphaGenome matched or exceeded the strongest external model in 25 of 26 variant-effect evaluations.
items.info: The main text also reports superiority in 22 of 24 genome-track prediction evaluations.
items.concl: The strongest claim is broad performance over diverse tasks, not perfection on every assay.

items.q: Why is non-coding variant interpretation difficult?
items.a: Non-coding variants can alter chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, transcription factor binding, contact structure, expression, and splicing, frequently in a cell-specific way.

items.q: What are the two fundamental compromises of earlier models?
items.a: Short-input models can resolve individual bases but miss distant regulatory elements; long-input models typically have coarser outputs. Models specialized for one regulatory modality cannot describe the full set of consequences of a variant.
items.info: The authors contrast ≤10 kb base-resolution methods with ~200–500 kb models often operating on 32- or 128-bp bins.

items.q: How is AlphaGenome different from Borzoi, Enformer, SpliceAI and Orca?
items.a: AlphaGenome jointly predicts numerous one-dimensional and two-dimensional modalities from a 1-Mb sequence, including detailed splice junctions and contact maps, rather than using separate specialist tools.
items.concl: Its design targets complementary strengths rather than a single narrow prediction task.

items.q: What biological outputs are predicted?
items.a: The human model predicts 5,930 tracks and the mouse model 1,128 tracks: gene expression (RNA-seq, CAGE and PRO-cap), splice sites, splice-site usage and junctions, DNase/ATAC accessibility, histone modifications, TF binding and DNA contact maps.
items.info: The paper presents 11 modality/output groups in Figure 1.

items.q: Why use a 1-Mb sequence window?
items.a: A long input provides local sequence motifs and long-range enhancer–promoter context. The authors cite a benchmark in which 465 of 471 validated enhancer–gene pairs fall within 1 Mb.

items.q: How is the architecture structured?
items.a: A U-Net-inspired encoder–transformer–decoder builds one-dimensional representations at 1-bp and 128-bp resolutions and two-dimensional representations at 2,048-bp resolution. Convolutions capture local patterns while transformers connect more distant regions.
items.info: The model uses sequence parallelism across eight connected TPU v3 devices during training.

items.q: How are splice junctions and contact maps represented?
items.a: Contact maps use two-dimensional genomic-pair representations; splice junction counts are produced by a dedicated mechanism that models donor–acceptor interactions rather than only per-base splice signals.

items.q: What are the two training stages?
items.a: Pretraining fits observed experimental genome tracks using fold-specific and all-fold models. Distillation trains one student model to match averaged predictions from all-fold teachers using augmented and mutated DNA sequences.
items.info: Held-out genomic intervals are used for fold-specific evaluation; the distilled all-fold student is used for variant-effect benchmarks.
items.concl: Distillation transfers ensemble behavior into one model for practical scoring.

items.q: How well does AlphaGenome predict experimental tracks?
items.a: It outperformed external benchmarks in 22/24 genome-track evaluations across all 11 predicted modality groups.
items.info: Reported examples include +14.7% relative improvement in cell-type-specific gene-expression log-fold changes versus Borzoi and +6.3% in contact-map correlation versus Orca.

items.q: How well does it predict variant effects?
items.a: The distilled model matched or outperformed competitors on 25/26 variant-effect tasks, spanning expression, splicing, polyadenylation, enhancer–gene links, accessibility and binding.
items.info: The reported eQTL direction improvement versus Borzoi is +25.5% relative.

items.q: Can AlphaGenome reconstruct multiple experimental signals at one locus?
items.a: In a held-out human chromosome 19 region, predicted RNA-seq, ATAC/DNase, histone, CTCF and contact patterns generally track corresponding experimental data.
items.info: Figure 2a shows a 1-Mb HepG2 example, and Figure 2b zooms into LDLR splicing.

items.q: How is transcript-level splicing represented in predictions?
items.a: The model predicts splice donor and acceptor positions, their usage, pairwise junction counts and RNA coverage, enabling a more complete picture of RNA processing than splice-site classification alone.
items.concl: Junction predictions can expose transcript structure changes invisible in site-only scoring.

items.q: How is gene-expression performance evaluated?
items.a: The authors compare expression across genes and across cell types or tissues using correlations, including normalized measures intended to isolate tissue-specific expression rather than overall gene abundance.

items.q: What kinds of splicing variants are tested?
items.a: The study tests splice-region and deep-intronic/missense variant effects, splice outlier status, sQTLs and massively parallel functional splicing assay variants, with zero-shot and supervised settings.

items.q: Why predict junctions instead of just splice donor or acceptor scores?
items.a: Variants can create or remove junctions and change competition between donor–acceptor combinations. Junction count predictions capture these outcomes, including events far from canonical splice-site dinucleotides.

items.q: How does AlphaGenome perform on splicing variant tests?
items.a: It achieves state-of-the-art performance on six of seven splicing variant benchmarks, with the strongest improvements often arising from composite or junction-based scores.
items.info: The paper reports the exception rather than claiming superiority in every splicing test.
items.concl: Splice junction modeling is a major source of the model’s advantage.

items.q: Which regulatory mechanisms are evaluated beyond splicing?
items.a: The paper evaluates variants affecting expression levels (eQTLs), distal enhancer–gene links, and alternative polyadenylation.

items.q: How are eQTL effects inferred from sequence?
items.a: The reference and alternative alleles are each inserted into sequence context; a gene-specific expression score is computed from their predicted differences and compared with observed QTL effect directions and effect sizes.
items.info: The paper also explores in silico mutagenesis for local sequence attribution.

items.q: What does the APOL4 example demonstrate?
items.a: At rs9610445, the alternative allele is associated with lower APOL4 expression, and AlphaGenome predicts the same direction in its gene-expression signal.
items.info: The example reports GTEx SuSiE posterior effect β = −0.709 and predicted variant score −1.52.

items.q: What is learned about tissue specificity and gene-distance effects?
items.a: AlphaGenome predicts eQTL effects more accurately than compared sequence models and assesses performance relative to variant distance from target-gene TSS; distal regulatory inference remains challenging.
items.concl: Gene-specific effects should be evaluated across relevant tissues, not only one aggregate track.

items.section: Performance across gene expression tasks – enhancer–gene linking
items.q: Can model attribution identify enhancers linked to genes?
items.a: The authors use sequence-derived sensitivity scores for gene expression to link candidate regulatory elements to their target genes without requiring a directly observed perturbation for every pair.
items.info: Comparisons include ENCODE-rE2G and distance-to-TSS baselines.

items.section: Performance across gene expression tasks – enhancer–gene linking
items.q: How well do model-derived links compare with supervised E2G methods?
items.a: Zero-shot AlphaGenome performs close to the extended ENCODE-rE2G supervised model, and adding AlphaGenome features to supervised linking improves performance across distance categories.
items.concl: Sequence-model features complement experimental enhancer–gene classifiers.

items.section: Improved prediction of 3′ polyadenylation QTL effects
items.q: How can AlphaGenome predict alternative polyadenylation without an APA-specific output?
items.a: By predicting RNA-seq coverage, the model implicitly captures alternative usage of proximal and distal polyadenylation sites; changes in predicted coverage can therefore score paQTLs.

items.section: Improved prediction of 3′ polyadenylation QTL effects
items.q: What are the results for APA and paQTLs?
items.a: The study reports APA Spearman ρ = 0.894 versus 0.790 for Borzoi. For paQTLs within 10 kb of a PAS, AUPRC is 0.629 versus 0.621; within 50 bp, 0.762 versus 0.727.
items.info: Both models perform worse as variants lie farther from polyadenylation sites.
items.concl: The same expression tracks support inference of 3′ end processing effects.

items.section: Improved prediction of chromatin accessibility, DNase sensitivity and binding QTLs
items.q: Which chromatin-related variant classes are evaluated?
items.a: The model predicts effects on chromatin accessibility (caQTLs), DNase sensitivity (dsQTLs) and transcription factor binding (bQTLs), using predicted differences between reference and alternative alleles.

items.section: Improved prediction of chromatin accessibility, DNase sensitivity and binding QTLs
items.q: How does it compare with ChromBPNet and Borzoi?
items.a: The paper reports better performance across the tested chromatin QTL classes and ancestries for causality and effect-size estimation.
items.info: Examples report Pearson r = 0.74 for fine-mapped caQTL effect sizes and r = 0.55 for SPI1 binding-QTL effects.

items.section: Improved prediction of chromatin accessibility, DNase sensitivity and binding QTLs
items.q: Can sequence attribution reveal the motif mechanism?
items.a: In silico mutagenesis highlights local sequence positions associated with predicted accessibility or TF-binding shifts, including NF-κB- and SPI1-related motifs.
items.concl: Attribution can suggest a regulatory mechanism but is not experimental validation.

items.section: Improved prediction of chromatin accessibility, DNase sensitivity and binding QTLs
items.q: What does the MPRA challenge show?
items.a: In the CAGI5 reporter assay task, combining model-derived scores across cell types and modalities with LASSO reaches Pearson r = 0.65, above scores using individual matched chromatin-accessibility tracks.
items.info: The paper gives r = 0.57 for matched DNase and r = 0.63 for all-cell DNase feature aggregation.

items.q: What cancer locus demonstrates the joint interpretation of variants?
items.a: The authors examine activating non-coding variants around TAL1 in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, including upstream neo-enhancer variants, an intronic SNV, and a downstream neo-enhancer.

items.q: What is predicted for an oncogenic TAL1 insertion?
items.a: For chr1:47239296:C>ACG, the model predicts higher H3K27ac/H3K4me1 near the mutation, changes in repressive and transcription-associated marks, and increased TAL1 RNA expression.
items.info: The predicted expression effect concerns TAL1 approximately 7.5 kb away; predictions use CD34+ common myeloid progenitor tracks as the closest available cellular context.
items.concl: The case study links local sequence change to chromatin and downstream expression in one analysis.

items.q: How does joint modality scoring help rank disease variants?
items.a: Combining local regulatory chromatin signals and target-gene expression identifies additional affected variants relative to either modality alone, with enrichment of known trait-altering variants among strong-scoring calls.

items.q: Why is 1 Mb of training context important?
items.a: The authors vary training and evaluation length to test how long-range context affects track and variant predictions. Their analysis supports training with long context to resolve distal regulation.

items.q: What is the effect of output resolution and distillation?
items.a: Ablations study prediction resolution and teacher-to-student distillation; fine-grained outputs and distillation contribute to accurate, robust variant scoring, rather than simply enlarging a sequence model.

items.q: Does multimodal training help specialized predictions?
items.a: Removing modalities or training solely on one type generally harms variant-effect prediction; expression and accessibility data provide especially large initial gains, with diminishing benefits from later modalities.
items.concl: Broad biological supervision improves learned DNA sequence representations.

items.q: What is the main interpretation of the paper?
items.a: A unified sequence model can predict several molecular consequences of regulatory variants from DNA alone, without requiring separate models for each assay.

items.q: What are key limitations?
items.a: Predictions depend on the human and mouse training context and measured assays; long-range elements outside the input window or biological states lacking matched training data can be difficult. Computational predictions are not direct causal experiments.
items.concl: A high model score is evidence for prioritization, not proof that a variant is causal.

items.q: What data are used to train AlphaGenome?
items.a: Human and mouse functional genomics tracks across gene expression, transcription initiation, splicing, accessibility, chromatin-associated features and contact assays, with track-specific preprocessing and targets.

items.q: How are unseen genomic regions evaluated?
items.a: Fold-specific models use genome interval partitions so test regions are held out, while all-fold models use the available training intervals to produce teacher predictions for distillation.

items.q: What is the general reference-versus-alternative scoring procedure?
items.a: For each variant, predict the selected track or gene output using reference and alternative sequence contexts; transform or summarize the difference into a score appropriate to the assessed modality.
items.info: The exact scoring window and aggregation differ for splicing, expression, accessibility, TF binding and E2G tasks.

items.q: What does in silico mutagenesis (ISM) measure?
items.a: ISM perturbs individual positions or local sequences computationally and evaluates resulting changes in model predictions to identify candidate functional motifs.
items.concl: ISM measures learned model sensitivity, not an experimentally measured binding event.

items.q: Why separate track prediction from variant effect prediction?
items.a: A model may fit observed genomic signal but still fail to predict the change caused by an allele; the authors therefore evaluate held-out tracks and independent QTL or functional variant benchmarks separately.
